analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover annual mammograms and prostate cancer screening tests.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to three House committees in July 1998 and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999, with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group health plans and insurers selling individual coverage to pay for yearly mammograms for women 40 and older and yearly prostate cancer screening for men 50 and older, with benefits modeled on what Medicare covers. It also barred insurers from denying enrollment or rewarding providers as a way to dodge the requirement. It was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, women 40 and older and men 50 and older with job-based or individual insurance would have been guaranteed coverage for annual mammograms or prostate screening, regardless of what their plan chose to cover, and could not be denied enrollment because they used the benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover annual screening mammograms for participants 40 and older and annual prostate cancer screening for men 50 and older, at a level comparable to Medicare's coverage of similar benefits.
Extends the same requirement to coverage sold in the individual market, so people buying their own insurance were protected too.

Bars plans from denying or dropping someone's enrollment solely to avoid paying for the screenings, and bars plans from paying individuals to give up the protection or penalizing or incentivizing providers to skimp on it.
Allowed insurers to keep normal deductibles and copayments, but prohibited cost-sharing that discriminates against the required screenings.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor health plans would bear the cost of the new mandated benefit, which would flow into premiums; screening providers would gain volume of covered tests.

drawbacks.text: Mandated benefits add to premium costs: insurers and the employers and individuals who pay premiums would absorb the cost of annual screening for a large share of the insured population.

The bill does not require anyone to get screened and explicitly allows plans to keep deductibles and coinsurance, so some people could still face out-of-pocket bills for the very tests the bill mandates coverage of.

Mandating annual screening for everyone over 40 or 50 imposes uniform testing regardless of individual risk, an approach that has been debated on grounds that broad annual screening finds conditions that may never have caused harm, leading to follow-up procedures and anxiety for some patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in their 40s and 50s with insurance, guaranteed coverage of cancer screening is a real, concrete benefit that many plans at the time did not provide or covered unevenly. The cost is higher premiums spread across all enrollees, and the bill's design has limits: it allows cost-sharing, relies on regulations to define what 'comparable to Medicare' means, and applies a one-size-fits-all screening schedule. On balance it is a straightforward patient-protection mandate whose main opposition would come from those paying for it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 1998, sent to three House committees, and referred to health subcommittees, but no committee ever acted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on July 24, 1998.
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — a split referral that requires any of the committees to act before the bill can move.

In late August 1998 the bill was referred to the Health subcommittee in one committee and the Health and Environment subcommittee in the other, and no further action was recorded before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans were better off, since they never had to absorb the cost of the mandated screening benefit. Insured women over 40 and men over 50 gained nothing; coverage of annual mammograms and prostate screening remained whatever their plan chose to offer.

for.name: Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three committees; it was her bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Tom Bliley, R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote and drew no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and committee inaction under Republican House control; no party positions were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill mandates a new covered benefit — annual mammograms and prostate screening — in both group and individual markets, and forbids workarounds like paying people to opt out. Insurers would bear the cost; without the bill, they keep coverage decisions in their own hands.
ERISA plans would have to add the screening benefit, raising plan costs; the bill grandfathers collectively bargained plans until existing contracts end, softening but not removing the cost.

A coverage mandate guarantees reimbursement for annual screening mammograms and prostate tests, expanding the volume of insured screening services. The bill explicitly leaves insurers free to negotiate reimbursement levels.
